lesson.title: Differential equations: order, degree, solutions and first-order methods

coverage.phrase: Solution of differential equations by method of separation of variables
Homogeneous differential equations of first order and first degree
Solutions of linear differential equation of the type dy/dx + Py = Q, where P and Q are functions of x or constants
Solutions of linear differential equation of the type dx/dy + Px = Q, where P and Q are functions of y or constants

blocks.text: What is a differential equation

An equation that contains an unknown function of one independent variable together with one or more of its **derivatives** is called an (ordinary) differential equation. Example: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y=0$.

Differential equations describe how a quantity changes: growth of a population, cooling, motion under a force. Solving one means finding the function $y=f(x)$ (or a relation between $x$ and $y$) which satisfies it for all $x$ in an interval.
Order and degree
The **order** of a differential equation is the order of the **highest order derivative** present in it.

The **degree** is the power (a positive integer) of the highest order derivative **after** the equation has been made a polynomial in its derivatives (free of fractional powers and of derivatives inside other functions). If the equation cannot be written as a polynomial in the derivatives, the degree is **not defined**.

blocks.caption: Order and degree of sample equations

blocks.text: Common mistake: reading the degree from the highest power of any derivative. Only the power of the **highest-order** derivative counts. In $\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^4$ the degree is $3$, not $4$.
General and particular solutions
A solution containing arbitrary constants. The general solution of an $n$th order equation contains exactly $n$ independent arbitrary constants. It represents a **family** of curves.
A solution obtained by giving particular values to the arbitrary constants, usually using given conditions such as $y(x_0)=y_0$ (initial condition). It represents a single curve of the family.
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x$ has general solution $y=x^2+C$. With the condition $y(1)=3$: $3=1+C\Rightarrow C=2$, giving the particular solution $y=x^2+2$.

**Forming a differential equation.** To find the equation of a family with $n$ arbitrary constants, differentiate the family $n$ times and eliminate the constants. For $y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-2x}$: $y'=2Ae^{2x}-2Be^{-2x}$ and $y''=4Ae^{2x}+4Be^{-2x}=4y$, so the equation is $y''-4y=0$ (order $2$ for two constants).
Separation of variables

If the equation can be written as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)\,g(y)$, rearrange to $\dfrac{dy}{g(y)}=f(x)\,dx$ so that all $y$-terms are on one side and all $x$-terms on the other, then integrate both sides: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{g(y)}=\int f(x)\,dx+C$.

blocks.solution: Separate: $\dfrac{dy}{y}=x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=\dfrac{x^2}2+C$. Using $y(0)=1$: $\ln1=0+C\Rightarrow C=0$. So $\ln y=\dfrac{x^2}2$, i.e. $y=e^{x^2/2}$.
$e^{x-y}=e^xe^{-y}$, so $e^y\,dy=e^x\,dx$. Integrate: $e^y=e^x+C$. Put $x=0,y=0$: $1=1+C\Rightarrow C=0$. Hence $e^y=e^x$, so $y=x$.

blocks.text: Homogeneous differential equations

A first-order equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=F(x,y)$ is **homogeneous** if $F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=F(x,y)$ for every $\lambda\ne0$, i.e. $F$ can be written as a function of $\dfrac yx$ alone. Example: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$, since the right side equals $\dfrac1{y/x}+\dfrac yx$.

Substitute $y=vx$ (so $v=\dfrac yx$). Then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. The equation becomes separable in $v$ and $x$. After integrating, replace $v$ by $\dfrac yx$. For equations of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy}=G\!\left(\dfrac xy\right)$, substitute $x=vy$ instead.

blocks.solution: Put $y=vx$: $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{x+vx}x=1+v$. So $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$, giving $dv=\dfrac{dx}x$. Integrate: $v=\ln|x|+C$. Replace $v=\dfrac yx$: $y=x\left(\ln|x|+C\right)$.
Put $y=vx$: $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=v+\tan v$, so $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\tan v$. Separate: $\cot v\,dv=\dfrac{dx}x$. Integrate: $\ln|\sin v|=\ln|x|+\ln|C|$, so $\sin v=Cx$. Hence $\sin\dfrac yx=Cx$.

blocks.text: Linear differential equations

An equation that is linear in the unknown function and its derivative. Standard forms: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$, where $P,Q$ are functions of $x$ (or constants); and $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+Px=Q$, where $P,Q$ are functions of $y$ (or constants).
For $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$. The integrating factor (I.F.) makes the left side the derivative of $y\cdot\text{I.F.}$. No constant is needed when finding $\int P\,dx$.
For $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+Px=Q$, with $P$ and $Q$ functions of $y$ only. The roles of $x$ and $y$ are swapped.

If the equation is not in standard form (for instance $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^2$), divide through by the coefficient of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ first: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac2xy=x$. Now $P=\dfrac2x$ and $Q=x$. Also use $e^{\ln f(x)}=f(x)$ when simplifying the integrating factor.

blocks.solution: Here $P=\dfrac1x$, $Q=x^2$. I.F. $=e^{\int\frac1x dx}=e^{\ln x}=x$. Then $yx=\int x^2\cdot x\,dx=\dfrac{x^4}4+C$. So $y=\dfrac{x^3}4+\dfrac Cx$.
This is of the form $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+Px=Q$ with $P=1$, $Q=y$. I.F. $=e^{\int1\,dy}=e^y$. Then $xe^y=\int ye^y\,dy=ye^y-e^y+C$ (by parts). So $x=y-1+Ce^{-y}$.

blocks.text: Number of arbitrary constants in the general solution equals the order. Degree is defined only when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives.

Choosing the method: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)$ $\Rightarrow$ separate variables; right side a function of $\dfrac yx$ $\Rightarrow$ homogeneous, $y=vx$; $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ $\Rightarrow$ I.F. $e^{\int P\,dx}$; $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+Px=Q$ $\Rightarrow$ I.F. $e^{\int P\,dy}$.
Exam tip: always write a linear equation in standard form before reading off $P$. In $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^2$ the I.F. is $e^{\int\frac2x dx}=x^2$, **not** $e^{\int2\,dx}$.

questions.stem: Highest derivative and its power: The order and degree of $\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^4+y=0$ are respectively
questions.explanation: The highest derivative present is $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so the order is $2$. The equation is a polynomial in the derivatives, and the power of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is $3$, so the degree is $3$.

optionRationale.2: The order is the order of the highest derivative (2), and the degree is its power (3); the numbers were swapped.
optionRationale.3: The highest order derivative is the second derivative, not the first.
optionRationale.4: The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative, which is 3, not the power of the first derivative.

questions.objective: Find the order and degree of a differential equation

questions.stem: The general solution of a third-order differential equation contains how many independent arbitrary constants?
questions.explanation: The general solution of an $n$th order differential equation has $n$ independent arbitrary constants, because roughly $n$ integrations are involved in recovering $y$ from its $n$th derivative, and each integration introduces one constant. For a third-order equation, $n=3$, so there are three constants.

optionRationale.1: One constant arises for a first-order equation, not a third-order one.
optionRationale.2: Two constants arise for a second-order equation.
optionRationale.4: The number of constants equals the order, which is 3.

questions.objective: Relate order to the number of arbitrary constants

questions.stem: The integrating factor of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=e^x$ is
questions.explanation: In $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ the integrating factor is $e^{\int P\,dx}$. Here $P=2$, so $\int2\,dx=2x$ and the integrating factor is $e^{2x}$.

optionRationale.1: This is the right-hand side Q, not the integrating factor e to the integral of P.
optionRationale.3: The integrating factor is an exponential: e to the power of the integral of P.
optionRationale.4: The sign of the exponent is wrong; the integrating factor is e to the integral of P, with P = 2.

questions.objective: Find the integrating factor of a linear equation

questions.stem: The curve of the family $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x$ that passes through the point $(1,3)$ is
questions.explanation: Integrate both sides with respect to $x$: $y=x^2+C$, the general solution (a family of parabolas). The curve through $(1,3)$ has $3=1^2+C$, so $C=2$. The particular solution is $y=x^2+2$.

optionRationale.2: This takes C = 3, ignoring the point: the condition y(1) = 3 gives 3 = 1 + C, so C = 2.
optionRationale.4: Its derivative is 2, not 2x; this is not a member of the family.

questions.objective: Find a particular solution from a point on the curve

questions.stem: Which of the following differential equations has its degree **not defined**?
questions.explanation: Degree is defined only when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives. In $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+\sin\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=0$ the derivative $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ appears inside a sine function, so the equation cannot be written as a polynomial in the derivatives. Its degree is not defined.

optionRationale.1: This is a polynomial in dy/dx, with degree 3.
optionRationale.2: This is a polynomial in the derivatives, with degree 1.
optionRationale.3: This is a polynomial in the derivative, with degree 2.

questions.objective: Identify when the degree is not defined

questions.stem: Separation of variables: The particular solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy$ with $y(0)=2$ is
questions.explanation: Separate: $\dfrac{dy}y=x\,dx$. Integrate: $\ln|y|=\dfrac{x^2}2+C$, so $y=Ae^{x^2/2}$ with $A=e^C$. At $x=0$, $y=2$: $2=A$. Thus $y=2e^{x^2/2}$.

optionRationale.1: The integral of x is x squared over 2, not x squared.
optionRationale.3: The constant enters as a factor, not as an added term: y = A e^{x^2/2}.
optionRationale.4: Integrating dy/y gives ln y, not y; the solution is exponential.

questions.objective: Solve a separable equation with an initial condition

questions.stem: Linear equation in x: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac yx=x^2$ is
questions.explanation: Standard form with $P=\dfrac1x$, $Q=x^2$. I.F. $=e^{\ln x}=x$. Then $xy=\int x^3dx=\dfrac{x^4}4+C$, so $y=\dfrac{x^3}4+\dfrac Cx$. Check by substitution: $y'+\dfrac yx=\dfrac{3x^2}4-\dfrac C{x^2}+\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac C{x^2}=x^2$.

optionRationale.1: The integral of x squared times the integrating factor x is x to the fourth over 4, not x cubed over 3.
optionRationale.2: Dividing by the integrating factor x also divides the constant: C / x.
optionRationale.4: The constant ends up as C / x because we divide by the integrating factor x.

questions.objective: Solve a linear equation dy/dx + Py = Q

questions.stem: Linear equation in y: The general solution of $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+x=y$ is
questions.explanation: Here $P=1$, $Q=y$ (functions of $y$). I.F. $=e^{\int1\,dy}=e^y$. $xe^y=\int ye^y\,dy=ye^y-e^y+C$. Dividing by $e^y$: $x=y-1+Ce^{-y}$.

optionRationale.1: Integrating y e^y by parts gives (y - 1) e^y, not (y + 1) e^y.
optionRationale.2: The factor e^{-y} arises from dividing by the integrating factor e^y.
optionRationale.3: The arbitrary constant is divided by the integrating factor, giving C e^{-y}.

questions.objective: Solve a linear equation dx/dy + Px = Q

questions.stem: Homogeneous equation: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}x$ is
questions.explanation: Put $y=vx$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. Then $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$, giving $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$, so $v=\ln|x|+C$. With $v=\dfrac yx$, $y=x\ln|x|+Cx$.

optionRationale.2: The constant multiplies x because y = vx with v = ln|x| + C.
optionRationale.3: The factor x multiplying ln|x| is missing; y = vx.
optionRationale.4: Substituting y = vx gives x dv/dx = 1, so v = ln|x| + C, not x.

questions.objective: Solve a homogeneous equation using y = vx

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative in it.
B. The degree is defined only if the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives.
C. The general solution of an $n$th order equation contains $n$ arbitrary constants.
D. A particular solution contains arbitrary constants.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is the definition of order. B is correct: degree needs a polynomial in the derivatives. C is correct: $n$ integrations give $n$ constants. D is wrong: a particular solution has the constants fixed by given conditions, so it has none left. So A, B and C are correct.

optionRationale.2: D is false, and B and C are also true, so A and D alone cannot be right.
optionRationale.3: D is false, and A is true, which this option leaves out.
optionRationale.4: D is false because a particular solution has no arbitrary constants.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on order, degree and solutions

questions.stem: Match the type of equation in List-I with the method of solution in List-II.
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)$ is separable, so separate the variables (A-I). $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=F\!\left(\dfrac yx\right)$ is homogeneous: put $y=vx$ (B-II). $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ uses the integrating factor $e^{\int P\,dx}$ (C-III). $\dfrac{dx}{dy}+Px=Q$ uses $e^{\int P\,dy}$ (D-IV).

optionRationale.2: It swaps the separable and homogeneous methods for A and B.
optionRationale.3: It swaps the integrating factors e^{∫P dx} and e^{∫P dy} for C and D.
optionRationale.4: It assigns the integrating factor to the separable equation and separation to the linear one.

questions.objective: Match equation types with solution methods

right: I. Separate the variables and integrate

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$ is homogeneous.
Reason (R): Its right-hand side can be written as a function of $\dfrac yx$ alone.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by $x^2$: $\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}=\dfrac{1+(y/x)^2}{y/x}$, which depends only on $\dfrac yx$. This is exactly the definition of a homogeneous first-order equation, so A is true and R is the correct explanation.

optionRationale.2: R is the definition of homogeneity applied to this equation, so it is the explanation.
optionRationale.3: R is true: the right side equals (1 + v squared)/v with v = y/x.
optionRationale.4: A is true, since the right side has degree zero in x and y.

questions.objective: Recognise a homogeneous equation

questions.stem: Exponential separation: The solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{x-y}$ with $y(0)=0$ is
questions.explanation: Write $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^xe^{-y}$ and separate: $e^y\,dy=e^x\,dx$. Integrate: $e^y=e^x+C$. With $y(0)=0$: $1=1+C$, so $C=0$. Then $e^y=e^x$ and $y=x$.

optionRationale.1: This results from integrating e^y dy as y instead of e^y.
optionRationale.3: This takes C = 1, but the condition y(0) = 0 gives e^0 = e^0 + C, so C = 0.
optionRationale.4: It fails the initial condition: at x = 0 it gives y = 1, not 0.

questions.objective: Separate variables with exponentials and apply an initial condition

questions.stem: Trigonometric integrating factor: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sec x$ is
questions.explanation: $P=\tan x$, so I.F. $=e^{\int\tan x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\sec x|}=\sec x$. Then $y\sec x=\int\sec x\cdot\sec x\,dx=\tan x+C$. Multiply by $\cos x$: $y=\sin x+C\cos x$.

optionRationale.1: Dividing by the integrating factor sec x multiplies the constant by cos x.
optionRationale.2: The integral of sec squared x is tan x; with I.F. sec x this gives y sec x = tan x + C.
optionRationale.4: y sec x = tan x + C gives y = sin x + C cos x after multiplying by cos x.

questions.objective: Solve a linear equation with a trigonometric integrating factor

questions.stem: Homogeneous with tangent: The general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac yx+\tan\dfrac yx$ is
questions.explanation: Put $y=vx$: $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=v+\tan v$, so $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\tan v$. Separate: $\cot v\,dv=\dfrac{dx}x$. Integrate: $\ln|\sin v|=\ln|x|+\ln|C|$, so $\sin v=Cx$, i.e. $\sin\dfrac yx=Cx$.

optionRationale.1: The separation gives cot v dv = dx/x, whose integral is ln sin v, not ln cos v.
optionRationale.2: The left side integrates cot v to ln sin v, not ln tan v.
optionRationale.3: ln sin v = ln x + ln C gives sin v = Cx, not C / x.

questions.objective: Solve a homogeneous equation involving a trigonometric function

questions.stem: Linear initial value problem: The solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=4x$ with $y(0)=1$ is
questions.explanation: I.F. $=e^{2x}$. $ye^{2x}=\int4xe^{2x}dx=2xe^{2x}-e^{2x}+C$ (by parts). So $y=2x-1+Ce^{-2x}$. The condition $y(0)=1$ gives $1=-1+C$, so $C=2$. Hence $y=2x-1+2e^{-2x}$. Check: $y'+2y=2-4e^{-2x}+4x-2+4e^{-2x}=4x$.

optionRationale.4: It does not satisfy the equation; the exponential term must be e^{-2x}.

questions.objective: Solve a linear initial value problem

questions.stem: The differential equation of the family of curves $y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{-2x}$, where $A,B$ are arbitrary constants, is
questions.explanation: $y'=2Ae^{2x}-2Be^{-2x}$ and $y''=4Ae^{2x}+4Be^{-2x}=4y$. Eliminating $A$ and $B$ gives $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-4y=0$. The order is $2$, matching the two arbitrary constants.

optionRationale.1: Differentiating twice gives 4y, so y double prime minus 4y = 0, not plus.
optionRationale.3: A first-order equation has only one constant; here there are two constants A and B, so the order is 2.
optionRationale.4: The second derivative equals 4y, since each exponential gains a factor 2 squared = 4.

questions.objective: Form a differential equation by eliminating constants

questions.stem: The differential equation of the family of parabolas $y^2=4ax$, where $a$ is an arbitrary constant, is
questions.explanation: Differentiate $y^2=4ax$: $2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4a$. Since $4a=\dfrac{y^2}x$, we get $2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y^2}x$, so (for $y\ne0$) $2x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$, i.e. $y=2x\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. One constant gives a first-order equation.

optionRationale.1: This is the equation of the family y = C x squared, not y squared = 4ax.
optionRationale.2: This comes from y squared = 2 x squared + C, not the given family.
optionRationale.4: This is a separable equation with solution y = C e^{x squared}, not a parabola.

questions.objective: Eliminate the parameter from a family of parabolas

questions.stem: Inverse tangent separation: The solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+y^2}{1+x^2}$ with $y(0)=\sqrt3$ is
questions.explanation: Separate: $\dfrac{dy}{1+y^2}=\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$. Integrate: $\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}x+C$. At $x=0$, $y=\sqrt3$: $\dfrac\pi3=0+C$. So $\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}x+\dfrac\pi3$; taking tangent and using $\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}$ gives $y=\dfrac{x+\sqrt3}{1-\sqrt3\,x}$.

optionRationale.1: This is tan(A - pi/3); the constant is +pi/3 because tan inverse of root 3 is pi/3.
optionRationale.2: The tangent addition formula has a minus sign in the denominator: 1 - tan A tan B.
optionRationale.3: This does not satisfy the equation: y prime = 1, but (1 + y squared)/(1 + x squared) is not 1.

questions.objective: Combine separation of variables with inverse tangent addition

questions.stem: If $y(x)$ satisfies $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=x^2$ for $x>0$ and $y(1)=1$, then $y(2)=$
questions.explanation: Standard form: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac2xy=x$. I.F. $=e^{2\ln x}=x^2$. $x^2y=\int x^3dx=\dfrac{x^4}4+C$, so $y=\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac C{x^2}$. From $y(1)=1$: $1=\dfrac14+C$, so $C=\dfrac34$. Then $y(2)=\dfrac44+\dfrac{3/4}4=1+\dfrac3{16}=\dfrac{19}{16}$.

optionRationale.2: This takes C = 1 instead of 3/4, giving 1 + 1/4; the condition y(1) = 1 forces C = 3/4.
optionRationale.3: This ignores the C / x squared term entirely.
optionRationale.4: This subtracts the C term (x squared / 4 - 3/(4 x squared)); it should be added.

questions.objective: Solve a linear initial value problem after converting to standard form
